other_side: Where NLW reads June's token budgets, Fable 5, and the scramble toward open weights as AI maturing into a real, cost-disciplined industry, Zitron reads the same month as the bubble's unit economics finally showing through. Seizing on the Bank for International Settlements' annual report, he notes the five largest hyperscalers are set to spend over a trillion dollars on AI capex across 2025-26, commitments that are "outpacing earnings and free cash flow" and forcing firms to issue debt. His warning is that disappointing returns could turn the capex boom into what the BIS calls a "protracted investment bust", cascading through indebted suppliers like Oracle and CoreWeave. To him, cheaper tokens and efficiency drives are not maturation but a sector discovering it cannot afford its own product.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is whether the enormous money flowing into AI compute converts into durable, defensible economic returns. Both accept two facts: hyperscaler capex is vast and currently outruns free cash flow, and providers are tightening per-token pricing after the subsidy phase. The empirical question that will resolve it is whether enterprises keep expanding AI spend at genuine positive return, or whether the big four guide capex down for lack of it; the observable that settles it is Q3-Q4 2026 hyperscaler capex guidance set against operating cash flow, plus any audited inference margin. What remains pure worldview is interpretation: Whittemore reads discipline and diversification as an industry maturing, Zitron reads the identical signals as the economics finally biting. NLW is vindicated if token efficiency and open weights let firms scale AI profitably; Zitron if financing pulls back into a bust. Both are polemicists with incentives, NLW bullish and builder-facing, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype, so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors, and here they agree the subsidy era is over. Watch the next capex guidance.
